Welcome to Pentland Field School
Pentland Field School is an all through school that meets the educational needs of children and young adults aged 4-19 with a range of learning disabilities including those who may be autistic and those who have physical or sensory needs.
Staff at Pentland Field School are committed to helping all pupils unlock their potential.
By supporting our pupils to make academic, social and emotional progress we hope they become young adults who know their own value can become active members of the communities in which they live.
Pentland Field School is a member of the Eden Academy Trust.
At Pentland Field we educate and support our pupils to become independent learners.
FIind out more about Pentland Field School
Our School
Our aim is that all our pupils develop a real love for learning.
How we learn
At Pentland Field we educate and support our pupils to become independent learners.
Parent information
Family Services supports families and promotes the well-being of our pupils.
News and events
We highlight meetings and dates on our website and via our Parent Newsletters.
Eden Academy Trust
Pentland Field School is part of a family of schools in the Eden Academy Trust.
Get in touch
If you would like to find out more about Pentland Field School, please feel free to contact us.
Our Approach and Curriculum
At Pentland Field School we focus on the individual learning needs of every pupil so that each pupil can reach their full potential.
At Pentland Field School therapy input and advice underpins and complements our curriculum, enabling pupils to access their education.
In Sixth Form, our aim is to “prepare (students) for adulthood”. Study programmes are based on securing positive outcomes for our students, and set solid foundations for adult life.
Family Services supports families and promotes the well-being of our pupils by encouraging social activities and provides a network of assistance and advice.

Our vision
At Pentland Field we aspire for our pupils to grow academically, socially and emotionally.
We aim for our learners to be well rounded and mature young adults, who know their own value and can contribute to the communities in which they live.
Our long term aims for pupils support this:
Communicate thoughts and needs appropriately
Making and maintaining relationships
Learn living skills that promote independence
Our values and our rules
Our school values align with our school rules. Together, they provide a frame of reference for what it means to work, learn, and live well.
Our values and rules belong to everyone – we agree to do our best to live by them, to acknowledge moments when we may have got that wrong, and seek to put that right.
When all in our school community agree to live this way, we model clearly for one another, and most especially to our pupils, what it looks like to take responsibility for yourself, and for others.
Our values are:
Courage
To do the right thing, and to take good risks when learning. That is how we grow.
Encourage
This is how we give courage to other people. It's part of how we take responsibility and show care for others.
Hope
What keeps us going when things seem too hard for us to manage. Change is often possible, and powerful when it happens.
Belonging
How we feel safe enough to try new things, and help others do the same. when we know we belong, we are helped to know we have intrinsic value. When we belong, we are more able to discover the things we are good at, our passion, and our purpose.
Growth
The key to unlocking potential, for ourselves, and in those around us.
Our rules align with our values
Our rules have been deliberately chosen to be as simple, clear and relevant as possible. Equally, the rules have enough breadth and depth to provide relevance for a wide range of scenarios that pupils will be likely to encounter, both in school and in the world beyond.
The school rules deliberately focus on just one word, so they can be understood by everyone.We have five core rules. everyone is taught about these, through phase assemblies and through clear modelling for each other. These are:
Help, Honest, Kind, Share, Listen
In addition, there are four other rules. These represent more complex themes, and are introduced and taught to pupils who have the capacity to understand them.
This means they can be introduced at any age, but that the level of understanding required to understand and follow them may not be understood by all pupils.
All staff also model these rules for our pupils. They are:
Gentle, Compromise, Strive, Forgive
Our school rules are selected for their relevance to our pupils, and for their flexibility across a range of situations.
They are important because they are key to progressing well through life’s journey. Our hope is that our values and our rules stay with our pupils long after they have left Pentland Field.

Further Careers information for parents
For further information, advice and guidance please see the below links or email mariam.fayeq@pentlandfieldschool.co.uk
Post 16 Transitions
While it is presumed that most pupils will remain at Pentland Field for the 6th form education, other options might be explored.
Parents and pupils will be invited to Preparing for Adulthood and Post 16 Options informations sessions, and will be offered a 1:1 Independent Advice and Guidance session to explore options.
The pupils working levels and predicted pathway in Pentland Fields post 16 will be shared with parents and pupils so all viable options can be looked into.
Post 19 Transitions
From the beginning of the post 16 journey we plan for the positive outcomes linked to life after Pentland Field. We know this can be a challenging and daunting time for parents and aim to make this process and stress and worry free as possible.
Through a series of information sessions and meetings we plan collaboratively for the pupils next steps. This involves visiting post 19 sessions, attending careers fairs and exploring options with the Independent careers adviser and the Job Centres Schools and Colleges Adviser.

Careers
At Pentland Field School the careers education acknowledges the eight Gatsby Benchmarks when planning for our Careers, Education, Information and Guidance (CEIAG) programme.
The CEIAG programme at Pentland Field School is reflective of the person-centred planning approach the school adapts when working within the Preparing for Adulthood framework.
Core Employability skills are incorporated across the curriculum and through the Skills Builder programme to promote and develop pupils skills, in preparation for whatever pathway they are on. These are skills not only for employment but for life.
Celebrating Success – Destinations Data
From year 9, we use annual reviews, Preparing for Adulthood meetings and 1:1 careers advice and guidance sessions to monitor students’ projected pathways and schedule interventions to ensure that they are on the pathway best suited to their skills, interests and ambitions.
This enables us to maximise the quality and choice of destination planning for students before they leave us.
Destination data informs us of the number of past students who have taken different routes and sustained those options.
Importantly it informs us about pupils who have not successfully sustained a placement on a chosen route, giving us insight over time as well as a better understanding of where our students go and what they do after leaving school at 16 or 18/19.
This helps to determine if the careers provision given to students was right for those individuals and feeds into the evaluation cycle.
Work-based learning is one of the most effective ways of preparing young people with SEN for employment
Work Experience
Students are expected to do work experience or some form of work-related training as part of their 16 to 19 study programmes, as appropriate to their needs.
At PFS we aim to broaden the employment horizons of all students by providing access to some type of work experience which is “relevant and meaningful”, using approaches such as:
Work-based learning is one of the most effective ways of preparing young people with SEN for employment. Our person centred approach to planning in Key Stage 3/4/5 ensures staff understand the student’s potential, abilities, interests and areas they want to develop.
This allows placements and opportunities to be carefully matched to students and informs honest conversations with potential employers and further education providers.
If you are an employer and are able to offer a workplace learning opportunity, please email mariam.fayeq@pentlandfieldschool.co.uk
By embedding the Benchmarks throughout our Study Programmes, our students will be better equipped and enabled to make their first successful steps into the world of work.
Encounters with Employers
Taster opportunities
External work based learning
Volunteering opportunities
Work shadowing
Exploring entrepreneurial options/Enterprise opportunities
Meeting the Gatsby Benchmarks
The Department for Education adopted the Gatsby Benchmarks as the best practice model for delivering effective careers provision. The Benchmarks are at the heart of the Government’s Careers Strategy, published in 2017, and form the framework for best practice and good embedded careers guidance.
By embedding the Benchmarks throughout our Study Programmes, our students will be better equipped and enabled to make their first successful steps into the world of work.
Independent Advice and Guidance
Pentland Field School is committed to providing students with high quality, independent advice and guidance with regards to careers, further and higher education and future life choices. Getting the right advice and guidance is an important part of school life in finding the right pathway at the end of Year 11 and Year 14.
To support this we are working with The Education Development Trust to access their employability and careers services, including specialist careers advice that is accessible and meets the needs of the young people within our setting. The career guidance sessions help us to give our students the information, advice and guidance they need to make informed choices for their future and are offered periodically throughout Key Stage 4 & 5.
Good career guidance can have a profound impact on social mobility, as it ensures that each and every young person, whatever their needs, background or ambitions, knows the options open to them to fulfil their potential.
The Careers Guidance Officer will explore options and advise young people and their parents on areas such as:
Through the schools careers programme, we have achieved some significant outcomes for our students, encouraging them to have high aspirations when planning their pathway through life. The person centred approach encourages pupils to share their dreams and aspirations for the future and the outcomes they achieve reflect this.

Further Careers information for employers
Throughout the careers programme, we want to facilitiate meaningful encounters with representatives from business, trips to factories, ‘careers talks’, collaborative projects and interactive work based learning sessions for pupils to provide an insight into the world of work.
These sessions may be face-to-face or, via virtual presentation. The overall organisation of the careers programme and work experience is undertaken by the school Careers Leader who liaises with the wider staff team to ensure the most relevant and engaging opportunities are offered appropriately to varying cohorts at Pentland Field.
If you are able to support students by working with us to provide any of these sessions please contact;
Mariam Fayeq, Transition and Careers Co-ordinator on 01895 806 520 or mariam.fayeq@pentlandfieldschool.co.uk
The experience that young people gain from workplace training can make them more attractive to employers.
Work Experience
Good work experience can often be the key to the door of a good job after leaving education: the more contact a young person has with the workplace, the more likely they are to find employment. This is especially true for young people with learning difficulties and disabilities. The experience that young people gain from workplace training can make them more attractive to employers.
We aim to provide work based learning which includes high quality contacts within the workplace with personalised work experience forming part of every study programme.
The benefits for employers employing a diverse workplace
Healthy, competitive businesses flourish where the needs of people, communities and businesses are interrelated. When given the opportunity, work experience students can achieve success in making a valuable contribution to a workplace. Increasingly, employers are recognising the importance of diversity in recruiting and retaining the skills and talent they need to be successful.
By getting involved in our work based learning programmes employers can be supported to create open and inclusive workplace cultures in which everyone feels valued and respected.
Competence and flexibility are vital skills that employers seek. Today more than ever, businesses need people with the ability to adapt to different situations and circumstances. Perhaps more than any group, people with disabilities can possess precisely these attributes.
On a daily basis, people with disabilities must think creatively about how to solve problems and accomplish tasks. In the workplace, this translates into innovative thinking, fresh ideas and varied approaches to confronting challenges and achieving success.
Further information on the benefits of employing a diverse workforce can be found here.
By becoming involved in provision for young people with learning difficulties and disabilites, you can expand your pool of talent, skills and creative business solutions.
Some of the key benefits to your business could include:
In return for offering a range of opportunities for our students we can offer:
Employers can be supported to create open and inclusive workplace cultures in which everyone feels valued and respected
Under health and safety law, work experience students are your employees. You treat them no differently to other young people you employ.
Your existing employers’ liability insurance policy will cover work placements provided your insurer is a member of the Association of British Insurers, or Lloyds, so there is no need for you to obtain any additional employer’s liability insurance if you take on work experience students.
The Business Disability Forum is a not for profit membership organisation that exists to transform the life chances of disabled people working through and with business to create a disability smart world.
Their Disability Smart Audit (sponsored by Unilever) is a whole-organisation disability management audit that has been developed to help organisations measure and improve on performance for disabled customers, clients or service users, employees and stakeholders.
Personal development opportunities for staff;
Improved staff retention;
Positive change to workplace culture and practice.
Advice on reasonable adjustments;
Advice on financial support and incentives; and
Free publicity for the business.

Further Careers information for pupils
It is important for all young people to stay in ‘learning’ after 16 and gain qualifications, skills or workplace experiences. However, it is important to remember that ‘learning’ can take place in different settings, including school, college, through work with training, bespoke programmes or even volunteering.
When looking at your options moving forward you will need to know what level you are currently working at to know what options and pathways are available for you. When exploring your options you can also think about distance and travel options.
Employment, Education, Training
Welcome to the Education, Employment and Training section of the website.
Young people say that getting a good job and earning money are important to them. It helps to develop a career plan based on what interests you. This section will give you some ideas, options and pathway suggestions to begin this important stage in your life.
Moving from school to college – advice and support
You will need to have a good transition from secondary school to college.
This is a very important transition and the earlier this is thought about, the better it will be.
Don’t be afraid to ask questions
No matter how silly you think they sound!
Do your research and look at the college website.
Things like what support they can offer you, their SEN Policy, Equality Objective and their SEN Information Report.
Post- 16 options
Further Education
Higher Education
Apprenticeships
Traineeships
Supported internships
Work and Learning (separately)
Work trial
Orchard Hill College
Orchard Hill College are a specialist college committed to offering social and vocational opportunities for students in the heart of their communities.
Uxbridge College
There are many courses and apprenticeships to choose from at Uxbridge College, ranging from level 1-level 4.
Foundation Learning & Skills for Life
Our courses are suitable for students who have few or no formal qualifications and would like to progress onto a vocational course in the future. They are suitable for people with special educational needs.
Traineeships
Participating in a Traineeship allows a young person to develop their skills and gain qualifications (including English and Maths for those who need it) whilst benefitting from high quality work experience. They can last from 6 weeks to 6 months and can be an ideal stepping stone to an apprenticeship and work.The work experience placement is not paid, but the costs of travel and lunch might be supported by the training provider or employer.Traineeships are suitable for those working at around Level 1 and who might benefit from additional support to prepare them for work.
A traineeship will put you in a better position to compete for an Apprenticeship or gain employment. Traineeships give you the opportunity to build your CV and get vital experience with local and national employers. Employers are at the centre of traineeships to ensure they give you the skills you need to secure a job and succeed in employment.
A traineeship is a training programme designed to prepare you for your future career, helping you to get ready for the world of work and improve your chances of getting an Apprenticeship or other job.Employers are at the centre of traineeships to ensure they give you the skills you need to secure a job and succeed in employment.
Supported Internships
Supported Internship programmes are available for young people aged 16-24 who have additional needs and hold an Education, Health and Care Plan and who wish to take their next steps towards employment.
Supported Internships are personalised study programmes, designed to better enable young people with learning difficulties and/or disabilities to achieve sustainable paid employment, by equipping them with the skills they require for the workplace.
They are available through several Post 16 FE providers and normally consist of a minimum of two days a week in a work placement and one day a week at college.
Students will have access to a Job Coach who will support them in the work place and work alongside the tutor whilst students are in college.
Supported Internships bridge the gap between education and employment, and help to improve independence and self-esteem.
If your child’s goal is to move into work they could join a Supported Internship, pre-apprenticeship programme or traineeship. Supported Internships are specifically for young people aged 16-24 with an EHCP. They are classified as ‘study programmes’ and are tailored to meet the needs of the young person and employer. Supported internships are offered by FE/Sixth form colleges and some independent training providers.
Reasonable Adjustments
All public sector services have a legal duty to make ‘reasonable adjustments’ to the way they make their services available to disabled people.
Employers are required to make reasonable adjustments to any elements of the job which place a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage compared to non-disabledpeople
Access to Work
An Access to Work (AtW) grant can pay for practical support if you have a disability, health or mental health condition to help you:
You can apply for support with:
Examples of the kind of help available through Access to Work are:
Find out more “Help and support for young disabled people to find and stay in work”
Start working

Move into self-employment or start a business

Other Benefits
Personal Independence Payment (PIP) is a benefit that helps with the extra costs of a long-term health condition or disability. It replaces Disability Living Allowance (DLA). Children turning 16 who currently claim DLA will be asked to claim PIP after their 16th birthday. This applies to all children turning 16 in England, Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland.

Curriculum
Pupils at Pentland Field school learn most effectively when they are able to learn together. Learning is a socially motivated, shared, collaborative experience.
Class sizes are small, currently averaging 10 or 11 pupils per class – with some slightly above or below this number.
A number of factors are considered when grouping pupils into a class: the age of the pupils, their developmental stage and level of emotional maturity at the time, their need for any specific environmental factors, their attainment at that point, and the way in which they communicate with peers.
By planning in this way, the school is aiming to create a social environment in which pupils participate in meaningful, shared learning experiences.
The curriculum is planned in a way that each phase of school Iife prepares pupils for the learning phase that follows next.
Pentland Field School makes provision for pupils with the following range of need:
Formal learners – The formal curriculum is taught as single, discrete subjects, covering: English, Maths, PE, Computing, Science, History, Geography, Art, Design technology and PSHE including RSE.
Semi-formal learners – The semi-formal curriculum covers: Maths, English, Computing, PE, PSHE including RSE, and Life Skills. Maths and English teaching focuses on both the academic knowledge and skills in the curriculum, and the Functional English and Maths key concepts and life skills needed by pupils in order to access the community. Topics are taught in an integrated way and includes Science, Art and Humanities.
The curriculum is planned so that each phase of school Iife prepares pupils for the learning phase that follows next.
Pentland Field School Curriculum Overview
Curriculum Policy
Learning is a socially motivated, shared, collaborative experience.
Early Years Foundation Stage and Key Stage 1
Our youngest pupils learn in a way that is sympathetic to some of the best principles of good early years teaching.
We recognise that learning delay means our pupils may need more time to learn in this way, in order to obtain all of the benefits of this.
Formal and Semi-formal pupils learn together. Exploration, discovery, and a structure that emulates a free-flow approach to learning will be in place for pupils of this age, where this is appropriate and practical to do so.
Pupils will continue to work in a way that offers plenty of socialisation and early play opportunities. Some learners may progress to formal learning at the end of Reception whilst others will continue to benefit from the practices of EYFS.
Gruffalo Autumn 2026 Curriculum Leaflet
Elmer Autumn 2026 Curriculum Leaflet
Pupils learn to adjust to the routines and expectations of school life
Key Stage 2
From year 3 onwards, pupils will follow the school’s core subject curriculum;
Pupils follow the school’s single-subject curriculum.A single-subject curriculum is extended through the school for pupils on the formal learning pathway from this point.
Teaching staff have the flexibility to teach in a formal or semi-formal way, according to the learning needs of the pupils they are teaching.
In many classes, a combination of approaches is required.
During this key stage, pupils learn to adjust to the routines and expectations of school life, gaining learning skills and basic skills in English and Maths that will support their learning for the rest of their time at school.
Picasso AUT 2026 Curriculum Leaflet
Jain AUT 2026 Curriculum Leaflet
Monet Autumn 2026 Curriculum Leaflet
Kusama Autumn 2026 Curriculum Leaflet
Key Stage 3
From year 7 onwards, the curriculum continues to follow the core, discrete and integrated learning structures. Some pupils will have matured to the point that they are able to benefit from a teaching delivery that is more formal in it’s approach. For others, it becomes clear that their developmental journey and type of learning needs means that they will continue to require a semi-formal approach to teaching and learning.
Careers planning begins to have more of a focus in KS3, in line with Gatsy Benchmark expectations, and pupils are helped and encouraged to take part in the Skills Builder programme, helping pupils to identify their strengths and areas for improvement.
By year 9, pupils will be actively included in Preparation for Adulthood planning, which is a part of the Annual Review process. This thread will continue for the rest of a pupil’s time at Pentland Field. Rigour in the curriculum means pupils are prepared for challenges at the next phase of schooling.

The Skills Builder programme helps pupils to identify their strengths and areas for improvement
Key Stage 4
From year 10, pupils learning the core curriculum begin an appropriate AQA unit certification or qualification and accreditation courses in English and Maths, ranging from Entry Level 1 to Entry Level 3.
Deciding which option to take is based on pupil knowledge and skill , and progress over time, and level of need. This then offers formal or semi-formal learning opportunities for pupils, with both pathways offering stretch and challenge for pupils, designed to move them forward based on what they need to learn next.
Pupils at KS4 have access to careers guidance, organised by the careers lead within the school. During this time, pupils and families are given relevant Information about possible further education options and providers for KS5, as well as signposting options for when many pupils will leave the school at the end of KS5.
Malala and Attenborough AUT 2026 Curriculum Leaflet
Nightingale Autumn 2026 Curriculum Leaflet
Key Stage 5
From year 12, the English and Maths curriculum offers Functional Skills Entry level 1 to Level for students in the Sisu Pathway. Students in the Ikigai and Ubuntu Pathways study Functional Literacy and Functional Numeracy. In addition, pupils in the Ikigai Pathway follow the Realising Aspirations programme.
All pupils follow a functional learning curriculum, which combines appropriately pitched academic rigour with preparation for life after Pentland Field, and as such focuses on key life skills.
Pupils are encouraged to match their learning with planning for the future. Pupils regularly spend time in the community, and are offered work experience placements.
To learn more about Key stage 5, please see our Post 16 section.
Ikigai AUT 2026 Curriculum Leaflet
Colosseum AUT 2026 Curriculum Leaflet
Sisu AUT 2026 Curriculum Leaflet
Life after Pentland​
The school plans carefully so that no pupils are left not without education, employment and training opportunities (NEET).
To learn more about life after Pentland, please see our careers section.

Post 16 Curriculum
The curriculum in Post-16 ensures that study programmes are designed to contribute to the student’s preparation for adulthood.
All students continue to study English and Mathematics. In Ubuntu Pathway and Ikigai Pathway this is referred to as Functional Literacy and Functional Numeracy. Literacy, language and numeracy skills embedded into a curriculum that supports the broadening and deepening of skills in a practical way.
For more information on the Functional Literacy and Functional Numeracy curriculum contents, please refer to the curriculum policy.
Study programmes following Sisu Pathway will complete Functional Skills – English and Mathematics (Entry 1 – Level 2) appropriate to the learners ability. Within Functional Skills English, students are assessed on reading, writing and speaking, listening and communicating. Within Functional Skills Mathematics, students will take a calculator, and non-calculator exam covering number, measure and data.
All Study Programmes are informed by aspirations in relation to the four areas of Preparing for Adulthood (including Employability, Good Health, Friendships, Relationships and Community and Independent Living) students working between Entry 1 – Entry 3 will complete ASDAN – Realising Aspirations modules to support the Preparing for Adulthood Curriculum.
Students are encouraged to participate in the Duke of Edinburgh Award. For more information on DofE click here.

Family services
Your Family Support Coordinator
Hello, my name is Gloria Ramshaw and I am Pentland Field School’s Family Services Coordinator.
My role in school is to provide support, advice and information to the families within our school community.
I can help you with any worries you may have concerning your child’s education, behaviour and wellbeing. I am also here to support parents with issues that may be impacting their family such as health or finances.
Advice and support are confidential, although concerns relating to safeguarding children will always be dealt with as per the school’s Safeguarding and Child Protection Policy.
I am also here as someone to talk to if you need it. I may not have all the answers, but hopefully, I can help you to work out how to find them.
This may be achieved through 1:1s or small group support. We also are very pleased to be supported by DASH a local charity for people with disabilities.
Emotional, practical and social support
Eden’s centralised Family Service team provide links between home, school and other services, to strengthen relationships and communication.
They work individually with families who need support, advice or guidance about statutory services involvement and those who are finding it difficult to manage their child’s behaviour or needs at home.
They also provide pupils and their families with a range of activities outside school hours so both pupils and their sibling and families have opportunities to socialise and have experiences otherwise inaccessible to them.
Support can include:
This list doesn’t include everything so please speak to me about anything worrying you or that you need support with.
coffee mornings at school
completing forms/applications
toileting issues
picky eaters
poor sleeping
setting boundaries
support to improve school attendance
Support for pupil attendance
If your child is finding school attendance difficult, you are not alone. Many children and young people with SEND experience challenges such as anxiety, sensory overload, or uncertainty about the school day.
The Eden Academy Trust provides practical guidance to help build routines, reduce stress, and support a positive, accessible school experience. Explore available resources here.
Regular activities
As well as our regular clubs we also offer a Summer Club during the first two weeks of the summer holidays and activity days out.
If you would like to find our more information about Family Services and information about clubs at Pentland Field School, please contact Gloria Ramshaw at: gloria.ramshaw@pentlandfieldschool.co.uk
After School Club – Wednesday 3.15-5pm
Youth Club – Thursday 3.15-7pm
How to get in touch:
I am based in school and can meet with you at school, at home, or even at a local coffee shop; we can meet at a time that works for both of us. You can get in touch by calling the school office on 01895 806 520 or you can email me at: gloria.ramshaw@pentlandfieldschool.co.uk
Please note: This is currently a part-time role so there may be a waiting list for any direct meetings. We may also need to prioritise support based on availability.
Contact Family Services:
Gloria Ramshaw
01895 806 520
gloria.ramshaw@pentlandfieldschool.co.uk
Looking for some extra help?
Here are details of some organisations which you may find useful as a support at home:
Contact a Family
A national charity for families with disabled children who provide information, advice and support.
ADHD Autism Harrow
Supports, educates and empowers individuals with ADHD and/or autism, their families, and the community.
DASH
Promotes independence and helping people with disabilities become more confident in life.
Equals
A national organisation for promoting the education of young people with severe learning difficulties. They provide a wide range of useful resource
National Autistic Society
The main charity for supporting individuals with autism and their families.
Hillingdon Carers
Local support group providing advice, information support and a broad range of services that help carers with their caring roles.
Priory Woods
A favourite site for our students. This site contains a large number of interactive games for young people with learning difficulties.
Scope
A disability organisation in England and Wales, particularly focusing on those with Cerebral Palsy.
Widgit
Home of the excellent ‘Writings with Symbols’ programme.

Lunch menu
We have high quality school meals, freshly made on our premises. The lunch menu operates on a 3-week rotation.
To view lunch menus, place an order and make payments, parents will require the Teachers2Parents app.
Families can order lunches up to 3 weeks in advance. Lunches must be ordered by midnight. Pupils not having school lunch should bring a healthy packed lunch. If you require any assistance please contact the schools admin team.
Please note, students wishing to observe religious practices, including, but not limited to, eating Halal foods should order the vegetarian option.
View the Autumn school meals menu here.
Healthy eating and snacks
Pentland Field School strongly encourages healthy eating. Food consumed in the school should be part of a broad and balanced diet. At snack times, students are encouraged to eat fruit. Through the School Fruit and Vegetable Scheme (SFVS) all 4-6 year olds receive a free piece of fruit or veg daily.

There are no minimum order quantities and your uniform will be delivered directly to your chosen address.
As well as our approved decorated school uniform, you are also able to order plain items such as trousers, skirts and shirts.

Our school champions the right of staff and students to embrace all Afro-hairstyles. We acknowledge that Afro-textured hair is an important part of our Black staff and students’ racial, ethnic, cultural, and religious identities, and requires specific styling for hair health and maintenance.
We welcome Afro-textured hair worn in all styles including, but not limited to, afros, locs, twists, braids, cornrows, fades, hair straightened through the application of heat or chemicals, weaves, wigs, headscarves, and wraps.
At this school, we recognise and celebrate our staff and students’ identities. We are a community built on an ethos of equality and respect where hair texture and style have no bearing on anyone’s ability to succeed.
